# Answer

## Verdict

The reviewer's inference does not follow. Candidate B's 0.9996 success and 1.004 retry
amplification are modeled outputs of a synthetic discrete-event queue model (C1). In that
model, success is a fraction of offered requests that complete before a deadline (C2), and
amplification is total attempts divided by offered requests (C3). Neither metric has a term
for a business effect, an idempotency key, an outcome record or a consumer deduplication
marker. The model's own failure-modes section says the queue model does not represent
business idempotency, and that retry-without-idempotency is outside its boundary and must be
recorded as a limitation rather than solved by a simulation parameter (C4).

The two numbers are therefore equally consistent with a path that never duplicates an effect
and with a path that duplicates on every retried attempt (C2, C3, C4; C12, C13). Removing the idempotency
requirement is not a modeled conclusion; it is a decision to accept an unmeasured
effect-integrity risk. The decision record must carry that risk as an explicit, unverified
constraint, together with the model boundary, layer-separated evidence statuses, the
duplicate-effect measurement gap, an explicit status, reversal triggers, residual risk and an
owner (C20). If removal is genuinely intended, it must be a superseding decision with
effect-level evidence or explicit owner acceptance, not a success number (C21).

**Layers and scope.** The question needs the modeling-and-simulation layer (scenario, run
and decision contracts) and the book layer (retry, idempotency and duplicate-effect
mechanism). The atlas was not needed: the question asks what a decision record must carry, not
which pattern owns duplicate suppression, and no pattern promotion or coverage claim is made
here. All section keys below were read through the session CLI against snapshot
4445fa068e7a0392182bb996f9e6c6dcd4dc0bdb6dd991fec215d020f2f8e04a.

## 2. What candidate B's numbers are

The comparison fixes a Poisson workload at 20 requests per second for 1,800 seconds after a
300-second warmup, uses 30 replications and a shared seed base, and changes only the candidate
configuration. B declares 12 servers, a 2-second timeout, three attempts, exponential backoff
with full jitter, a 240-request bulkhead and a relative cost of 8.0 (C1). Its reported result
is success 0.9996 (95% CI 0.9995-0.9997), p95 1.206 s, cost 1.34 and timeout 0.0041; A is
0.9218 with amplification 1.000; C is 0.9679 with 1.079 (C1). The comparison is synthetic:
the confidence intervals are narrow because the workload is synthetic and the replications are
independent, and narrow intervals do not make the inputs measured (C13). The run is converged
and replayable; replay would show that the stored inputs, engine version and seed produce the
stored metrics, not that the model is valid (C13).

## 3. Why the metrics cannot speak to duplicate effects

Six independent reasons, each sufficient on its own: the metric's unit is wrong, the quantity
is wrong, the model has no effect state, the boundary excludes the mechanism by declaration,
the evidence layer forbids the inference, and the metric is observationally constant across
safe and unsafe worlds.

### 3.1 The success unit is a request, not an effect

The success rate is defined over offered requests. In the overload example, A "succeeds on
0.6488 of offered requests; 0.3495 time out and 0.0005 are rejected" (C2). The discrete-event
conservation check is "offered = completed + rejected + failed + in_system" (C2). Every offered
request is counted once, and a request that completes is one success no matter how many
business effects it applied. If every successful request applied its effect twice, the
identity would still balance and success would still be 0.9996. Duplicate effects are not a
noisier version of a modeled quantity; they are a different unit that the numerator never
counts.

### 3.2 Amplification is a load ratio, not an integrity ratio

Amplification is "total attempts divided by offered requests" (C3). The page's own gloss is
that 1.05 attempts per request means 5% more load (C3). So 1.004 means B's retry layer adds
0.4% attempts relative to offered requests. That is a genuine capacity statement: B's retries
do not materially raise load, unlike C's 1.079. But it bounds attempts, not their outcome.
The model does not know whether the timed-out attempt it is retrying had committed; a retry
after an uncommitted attempt and a retry after a committed-but-unacknowledged attempt are the
same transition (C4, C5). "Safe" in the retry-budget sentence means capacity-safe; "safe" in
the idempotency requirement means effect-safe. The reviewer equivocates between the two.

### 3.3 The model has no effect state

The model's state is the request. Its scope is "request admission, a bounded queue, a server
pool, per-attempt deadlines and bounded retries"; excluded are "dependency calls, storage,
network and deployment" (C11). The resource state is exactly a fixed number of servers, a
FIFO queue with a capacity, a bulkhead, a per-attempt timeout and a bounded retry budget
(C24). The engine does not implement even priority or preemption; a model that needs them
requires a new contract and new tests, not an undocumented flag (C24). An effect ledger and a
dedup marker would be additions of the same kind: new state, new contract, new tests. There
is no key store, outcome record, dedup marker, consumer or effect ledger, so no derived
metric can be an effect metric. Conservation is "necessary but
not sufficient" even for assigning requests to outcomes (C2); it cannot see an effect at all.
This is a representation limit, not a statistical one: adding replications or narrowing the
interval cannot create a variable the engine never carries.

### 3.4 The boundary excludes idempotency by declaration

The exclusion is declared, not incidental. The failure-modes list names "Retry without
idempotency": "A timed-out request may have committed an effect; the retry duplicates it. The
queue model does not represent business idempotency." It then says these failure modes are
"outside the queue model's boundary" and "must be recorded as limitations, not solved by a
simulation parameter" (C4). The scope rule allows an omission only if "the omitted parts cannot
change the comparison under the declared conditions" (C11). An effect-integrity constraint can
eliminate a candidate or reverse a recommendation; a boundary mismatch can reverse the result
(C11). A calibrated model can produce a simulation result that does not support the decision
because a hard constraint was omitted (C12). This omission is material, not cosmetic.

### 3.5 The evidence layer forbids the inference

V12 separates five layers: source and claim evidence, model verification, calibration,
simulation evidence and decision evidence (C12). A model can be verified without being
calibrated; V12 has no operational validation against a real system, and every model is
uncalibrated (C12). Replay proves reproducibility, not validity, measured inputs or a correct
decision (C13); more replications make an assumption more precise, not more representative
(C13). The explicitly forbidden inferences include "The simulation succeeded, so production
will succeed" and "The decision record recommends B, so B is safe to deploy" (C19). The
reviewer's inference is the second one: a model success number is being used as a
deployment-safety certificate.

### 3.6 Observational equivalence: 0.9996 is constant across safe and unsafe worlds

Consider two worlds that share the scenario, seed and engine. In W_safe the publish effect is
naturally idempotent, keyed or deduplicated, so no retry re-applies an effect. In W_dup every
retry of a timed-out attempt that had committed re-applies it. The engine's transitions never
consult an effect ledger, so both worlds produce the same offered/completed/failed/attempt
counts, the same p95, the same cost and the same 0.9996/1.004. The likelihood of the observed
metrics is identical under W_safe and W_dup. A metric that is constant across a hypothesis and
its negation has no diagnostic value for that hypothesis; the 95% CI quantifies sampling error
around a quantity that cannot separate the worlds.

This equivalence is my inference from the model definitions (C2, C3, C4), not a sentence in
the sources. It is the precise sense in which the metrics "say nothing": not that they are
noisy, but that the measured quantity is blind to the effect layer. A test whose outcome is
the same whether the requirement is met or violated cannot justify removing the requirement.

### 3.7 The success gain and the duplicate exposure are the same mechanism

B's advantage over A is produced by retrying deadline misses: A 0.9218 with one attempt, B
0.9996 with three (C1). A deadline miss is the model's representation of an attempt whose
outcome is unknown; outside the model, that is exactly the state in which the effect may
already be committed (C5). The retry that converts a miss into a success can also re-apply
the effect. The model credits the recovery and has no term for the possible second
application. The more the retry budget improves success, the more this ambiguity has been
exercised, not resolved. That is why the success number cannot be evidence for effect safety
even in the direction one might expect.

## 4. What a duplicate effect is on a publish path

On a publish path the effect is a state change visible outside the request. The idempotency
page's central failure: "After an acknowledgment is lost, a new identity can duplicate a
committed effect" (C5). A timeout "is not evidence that the external job did not start" (C5),
and cancellation is not proof that a committed effect was undone (C5). Publication adds
re-delivery: the practical contract is at-least-once delivery plus consumer idempotency; the
same event keeps identity E on redelivery; a broker's producer idempotence cannot make an
unrelated consumer's external side effect globally exactly once (C8). The dedup marker must
commit in the same consumer transaction as the effect, or the alternative must be demonstrated
(C8).

The positive requirement is the idempotency contract: one logical intent, caller/payload
scope, retention window, an outcome record checked atomically with the effect, duplicate
returns the recorded outcome, and the guarantee ends at key expiry (C7). Retry budgets and
backoff are not a substitute: "no combination makes non-idempotent effects safe by itself"
(C6), and "Backoff does not make a non-idempotent effect safe" (C6). A migration or replay
path adds late arrivals and re-delivery; the V12 migration chapter explicitly does not model
record-level reconciliation or schema compatibility, and treats assumed inputs as a reason for
insufficient evidence (C18).

## 5. What the decision record must carry instead

At minimum the record must carry the following, with the idempotency requirement itself in
the constraints block rather than in the metrics block.

1. **The requirement as a constraint.** A constraint entry with a statement, scope and owner:
   every state-changing publish is idempotent under retry and redelivery for the declared
   effect scope. The statement should reference the key/intent identity, caller and payload
   scope, retention, atomic outcome record, duplicate response, conflict response and
   inspectable record, or the alternative (natural idempotency, unique constraint,
   compare-and-set, single writer) (C7, C9, C10). A hard constraint and a non-quantitative
   constraint are different fields; the model cannot measure either (C10).
2. **The model boundary and limitation.** The record must say, next to the metrics, that
   success and amplification are request/attempt quantities and that business idempotency is
   outside the queue model's boundary. The failure mode "retry without idempotency" is a
   limitation, not a simulation parameter (C4, C11). The record must also carry the validity
   limits: valid only for the synthetic workload; no dependency calls or storage in the
   checkout model; no production claim without measurement; and a validity limit is a condition
   on the result's use, not a disclaimer, so a decision that needs the omitted mechanism is
   outside the model's domain (C25).
3. **Layer-separated evidence statuses.** Model verification, calibration, simulation and
   source evidence are separate; duplicate-effect evidence is unknown/absent, not "assumed
   zero". The model is uncalibrated and the success number is modeled (C12, C14).
4. **The measurement and test gap.** The record must carry the duplicate-effect measurement
   plan and its execution status: count logical intents, transmitted attempts, accepted
   effects, duplicate observable side effects and unresolved outcomes separately, with the
   adversarial cases (same key and different payload, lost acknowledgment after commit, crash
   around the atomic record, two consumers, replay after key expiry, downstream effect without
   readback) and the acceptance criterion (C17, C8). The source says no such tests have been
   executed for the idempotency chapter (C17).
5. **An explicit outcome and status.** The status is one of proposed, decision-supported,
   insufficient-evidence or rejected (C14). If the constraint is hard and cannot be evaluated
   by the model, the correct outcome is insufficient evidence; if it is non-quantitative and
   unverified, a conditional recommendation is possible only with the condition stated.
   Neither outcome is "safe" (C15, C10).
6. **Reversal triggers and what would change the outcome.** The record must name the
   measurement, the range that would support or reject the decision, the owner, the
   consequence of staying in the current state and the review trigger (C15). For this
   decision that includes a measured duplicate rate, a measured retry or acknowledgment-loss
   rate materially above the modeled value, a key retention shorter than the retry and replay
   horizon, or a consumer without deduplication (C14, C15).
7. **Residual risk and the consequence of being wrong.** A duplicate effect can be
   irreversible while a skipped launch is detectable; where the outcomes are not equally
   recoverable, the source's general preference is to fail closed, and that choice must be
   recorded as a policy decision rather than hidden in a metric (C23, C15).
8. **Provenance and non-claims.** Model and scenario hashes, engine version, seeds,
   replications, limitations and result hash belong to the run record; replay proves
   reproducibility, not truth; the record must not claim production validity, CI execution,
   owner acceptance or pattern promotion (C13, C12).
9. **Metric-set discipline.** A decision record cannot use a metric not declared in the
   scenario (C19). Duplicate rate is not in the candidate-B scenario's metric list (success
   rate, p95 latency, throughput, cost per 1000 successes, rejection rate and retry
   amplification) (C19), so it must be carried as a constraint or unknown, not invented as a
   modeled metric.
10. **A superseding decision if removal is intended.** Removing a hard constraint is a new
    decision, not a metric consequence: it needs evidence that the effect is duplicate-safe
    (natural idempotency, uniqueness or conditional write, single writer, consumer dedup with
    retention) or an explicit owner-accepted risk with rationale, residual risk and expiry
    (C21, C16). The status field makes that change visible; a plan edit alone bypasses the
    record.

A migration plan is not the decision record. If the requirement lives in the plan, the plan
must reference the decision record's constraint and its verification gate. Removing it from
the plan without a superseding record would bypass the constraint, the evidence status and the
reversal triggers at once.

## 6. What would legitimately justify removing the requirement

Legitimate routes to removal are effect-level, not load-level:

- the effect is naturally idempotent or protected by a uniqueness constraint, compare-and-set
  or single writer, so a retry cannot apply it twice (C7);
- the consumer deduplicates and the marker commits with the effect, with retention covering
  the retry and replay horizon (C8, C7);
- executed adversarial tests show no duplicate observable effect within a declared tolerance,
  and the duplicate-rate measurement supports the declared range (C17, C15);
- the owner explicitly accepts the residual risk, with rationale, consequence and review
  trigger (C15, C21).

None of these is a success or amplification number. What would not justify removal: more
replications or a narrower confidence interval (C13), a lower amplification (C3), a higher
success rate (C2), a matching replay (C13), or the absence of duplicate observations in a
model that has no duplicate observable (C4).

## 7. What the model does establish, and the record discipline it still needs

The model does establish something useful: under the synthetic workload, B completes more
requests and costs less per success than A, and its retry load is far below C's. That is a
legitimate input to the capacity and completion decision, and it is legitimate to recommend B
on those grounds with the operability constraint still unverified (C10). What it cannot do is
adjudicate effect identity.

The worked example's reversal list already has the right shape: a measured retry rate
materially above the modeled value, a measured p95 tail, a cost-weight change and a failed
operability review; a narrower confidence interval would not reverse it (C14). One
record-discipline defect is visible in the book itself: the worked example sets the reversal
threshold at a modeled retry rate of 1.003, while the retry page reports B's amplification as
1.004 (C22). A decision record must bind one versioned value and state which one the trigger
uses; otherwise a reviewer cannot tell whether the observed 1.004 is already outside the
declared range. The inconsistency is small, but it is exactly the kind of thing the record
exists to prevent.

## 9. Unknowns, contradictions and limits

The decisive quantity, the duplicate-effect rate of the publish path under real retry,
redelivery and replay behavior, is unknown in this evidence. No adversarial test of the kind
the chapter specifies has been executed (C17), and I found no production duplicate
measurement in the sections read; a zero-result search does not prove absence. The consumer deduplication implementation, the key retention window relative to
the retry and replay horizon, and whether every consumer applies the effect idempotently are
all unverified in this evidence. I did not read the actual migration plan or the decision
record artifact; only the contracts, the worked example and the mechanism pages were read.
The specific publish operation's acknowledgment-loss and commit behavior was not observed: the
sources establish the general failure mode, not this system's exposure. The model's retry path
is taken from the page text and state diagram; I did not read the engine source, so the exact
attempt accounting is not independently verified here.

Contradiction to resolve: the worked example's reversal trigger says the modeled retry rate is
1.003, while the retry-amplification page reports B at 1.004 (C22). No claim of production
behavior, independent review, CI execution, owner acceptance or pattern promotion is made.
